ms_math_t12_st01.title: Reflection
ms_math_t12_st01.overview: A reflection creates a mirror image of a shape across a fixed line called the line of reflection. The image has the same side lengths and angles as the original, but its orientation is reversed. The exact coordinate changes depend on the mirror line.

details: The line of reflection acts as a mirror. It is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining any point and its reflected image.
Common mirror lines include the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis, and diagonal lines such as $y=x$.
Any point that lies on the mirror line stays in the same position after reflection.
**Across $x$-axis ($y=0$):** Flip the sign of $y$. $(x, y) \rightarrow (x, -y)$.
**Across $y$-axis ($x=0$):** Flip the sign of $x$. $(x, y) \rightarrow (-x, y)$.
**Across $y=x$ (Diagonal):** Swap $x$ and $y$. $(x, y) \rightarrow (y, x)$.
Reflection is a rigid transformation. The side lengths, angles, and area of the shape do NOT change. Only the orientation (facing direction) is reversed.

worked_examples.problem: Reflect the point $P(4, 2)$ across the $y$-axis.
solution_steps: Step 1: Identify the rule for reflecting across the $y$-axis: $(x, y) \rightarrow (-x, y)$.
Step 2: Take the original coordinates $P(4, 2)$.
Step 3: Flip the sign of the $x$-coordinate. $4$ becomes $-4$. The $y$ stays the same.
Step 4: The new point is $P'(-4, 2)$.

worked_examples.problem: Reflect the point $Q(3, 5)$ across the diagonal line $y = x$.
solution_steps: Step 1: Identify the rule for reflecting across $y=x$: $(x, y) \rightarrow (y, x)$.
Step 2: Take the original coordinates $Q(3, 5)$.
Step 3: Simply swap the $x$ and $y$ values.
Step 4: The new point is $Q'(5, 3)$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Flipping both coordinates for a single-axis reflection.
common_mistakes.correction: When reflecting across the $x$-axis, ONLY change the $y$ sign. Changing both $(-x, -y)$ is actually a $180^\circ$ rotation, not a reflection.

quick_summary: Reflection acts like a mirror across a fixed line.
To reflect over the $x$-axis, change the sign of $y$.
To reflect over the $y$-axis, change the sign of $x$.
The shape stays the same size, but its orientation is reversed.

ms_math_t12_st02.title: Lines of symmetry
ms_math_t12_st02.overview: A line of symmetry is a line along which a shape can be reflected onto itself. It divides the shape into two matching mirror-image halves. Some shapes have no lines of symmetry, some have a finite number, and a circle has infinitely many.

details: Imagine folding the shape along the proposed line. The two halves must overlap exactly.
Equivalently, reflecting the whole shape across that line leaves the shape unchanged.
For **Regular** polygons (where all sides and angles are perfectly equal), the number of lines of symmetry is exactly equal to the number of sides ($n$).
A regular pentagon has 5 sides and 5 lines of symmetry. A square has 4 sides and 4 lines of symmetry.
A non-square rectangle has exactly 2 lines of symmetry: the horizontal and vertical lines through its centre. Its diagonals are not lines of symmetry.
A scalene triangle has 0 lines of symmetry.
A general parallelogram that is neither a rectangle nor a rhombus has no line of reflection symmetry.

visual_aids.title: Symmetry in Quadrilaterals
visual_aids.caption: A square has 4 lines of symmetry, but a rectangle only has 2. Diagonals do not work for rectangles!
visual_aids.alt_text: Visual showing a square and a rectangle. The square has 4 dashed symmetry lines (vertical, horizontal, 2 diagonals). The rectangle has 2 dashed symmetry lines (vertical, horizontal).

worked_examples.problem: How many lines of symmetry does a regular hexagon have?
solution_steps: Step 1: Identify the shape. It is a 'regular' polygon.
Step 2: A hexagon has $6$ sides.
Step 3: Because it is regular, the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides.

worked_examples.problem: Does a standard parallelogram (that is not a rectangle or rhombus) have any lines of symmetry?
solution_steps: Step 1: If you fold a slanted parallelogram vertically or horizontally, the corners will stick out and not match.
Step 2: If you fold it diagonally, the points will point in opposite directions.
Step 3: Therefore, it has no fold lines that create perfect mirror halves.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking a rectangle has 4 lines of symmetry.
common_mistakes.correction: Many students think you can fold a rectangle diagonally (corner to corner). If you try this with a piece of paper, the corners will not line up. Only squares have diagonal symmetry.

quick_summary: A line of symmetry folds a shape into two identical mirror halves.
Regular Polygons: Lines of symmetry = Number of sides ($n$).
Circle: Infinite lines of symmetry.

ms_math_t12_st03.title: Rotational symmetry
ms_math_t12_st03.overview: A shape has rotational symmetry if it matches its original appearance after a rotation through an angle greater than 0° and less than 360° about a fixed centre. The centre stays fixed while every point of the shape moves around it.

details: A shape has rotational symmetry if it matches its original outline at least once *during* the spin, before returning to the start ($360^\circ$).
A square matches itself 4 times during a spin (at $90^\circ, 180^\circ, 270^\circ,$ and $360^\circ$).
The centre of rotation is the fixed point about which the shape turns. Every point of the shape follows a circular path centred on this point.

key_concepts.definition: A half-turn about the diagonal intersection.
details: A parallelogram that is neither a rectangle nor a rhombus has no line of reflection symmetry.
Every parallelogram has rotational symmetry of order 2: a rotation of $180^\circ$ about the intersection of its diagonals maps it onto itself.
Rectangles, rhombi and squares also have this $180^\circ$ rotational symmetry; some of these special parallelograms also have reflection symmetry.

worked_examples.problem: Does a non-square rectangle have rotational symmetry? If so, at what angles?
solution_steps: Step 1: A non-square rectangle does not match itself after a $90^\circ$ turn.
Step 2: After a $180^\circ$ turn about its centre, it matches its original outline.
Step 3: It returns to its starting orientation at $360^\circ$, which completes the full turn.
worked_examples.final_answer: Yes. It matches after a $180^\circ$ turn (and returns to its starting position at $360^\circ$).

worked_examples.problem: Does an isosceles triangle (not equilateral) have rotational symmetry?
solution_steps: Step 1: An isosceles triangle is tall and pointy at the top.
Step 2: If you spin it, the point moves to the side, then the bottom, then the other side. It never matches the original outline until it gets all the way back to the top at $360^\circ$.
Step 3: Because it doesn't match at any angle *less* than $360^\circ$, it has no rotational symmetry.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking shapes with line symmetry always have rotational symmetry.
common_mistakes.correction: An isosceles triangle or a kite has a line of symmetry (you can fold it in half), but it has NO rotational symmetry. If you spin it upside down, it looks completely different.

quick_summary: Rotational symmetry means a shape matches itself after a turn greater than $0^\circ$ and less than $360^\circ$.
A non-equilateral isosceles triangle has no non-trivial rotational symmetry.
Every parallelogram has $180^\circ$ rotational symmetry about the intersection of its diagonals; a generic parallelogram has no line of reflection symmetry.

ms_math_t12_st04.title: Order of rotational symmetry
ms_math_t12_st04.overview: The order of rotational symmetry is the number of times a shape matches its original outline during one complete $360^\circ$ turn. Count each matching position once; the starting position and the final $360^\circ$ position are the same orientation.

details: Turn the shape through one complete $360^\circ$ revolution and count the matching positions, counting the return to the starting orientation only once.
If the shape matches only when the full $360^\circ$ turn is complete, its order is $1$.
For regular polygons, the order of rotational symmetry is always exactly equal to the number of sides ($n$).
A regular octagon has an order of $8$.
The smallest positive angle that maps the shape exactly onto itself is the smallest angle of rotation.
Divide $360^\circ$ by this angle to find the order: $\text{Order}=\frac{360^\circ}{\text{Smallest angle}}$.

worked_examples.problem: A regular hexagon has rotational symmetry. Find its order and the smallest angle of rotation.
solution_steps: Step 1: A regular hexagon has $6$ sides. Because it is regular, its Order is $6$.
Step 2: Find the smallest angle by dividing $360^\circ$ by the order.
Step 3: $360^\circ \div 6 = 60^\circ$.

worked_examples.problem: A shape matches its original position after every $45^\circ$ rotation. Find its order.
solution_steps: Step 1: Use the formula: $\text{Order} = \frac{360^\circ}{\text{Smallest Angle}}$.

common_mistakes.correction: The starting position ($0^\circ$) and the final full-turn position ($360^\circ$) are the exact same spot. You only count it once, not twice.

quick_summary: Order = How many times the shape matches itself in a $360^\circ$ spin.
Smallest Angle $= 360^\circ \div \text{Order}$.
A standard rectangle has an order of 2 ($180^\circ, 360^\circ$).

ms_math_t12_st05.title: Translation
ms_math_t12_st05.overview: A translation is a geometric 'slide'. It moves every single point of a shape the exact same distance in the exact same direction, without spinning, resizing, or flipping it. It is like pushing a box across the floor.

details: A translation only changes the position of the shape. It preserves lengths, angles, area, and perimeter.
The original shape and the translated image are perfectly congruent.
Translations are often written as column vectors: $\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$.
The top number is the horizontal movement (Positive = Right, Negative = Left).
The bottom number is the vertical movement (Positive = Up, Negative = Down).
To translate a point $(x, y)$ by a vector $\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix}$, just add the numbers: $(x+a, y+b)$.

worked_examples.problem: Point $A(2, 5)$ is translated by the vector $\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$. Find the new coordinates of $A'$.
solution_steps: Step 1: The vector tells us to subtract $3$ from $x$ (move left $3$), and add $4$ to $y$ (move up $4$).
Step 3: $y_{\text{new}} = 5 + 4 = 9$.

worked_examples.problem: A point moves from $P(1, 2)$ to $P'(5, -1)$. What is the translation vector?
solution_steps: Step 1: Find the change in $x$: $5 - 1 = +4$ (Right 4).
Step 2: Find the change in $y$: $-1 - 2 = -3$ (Down 3).
Step 3: Write it as a column vector.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing the $x$ and $y$ numbers in the vector.
common_mistakes.correction: Just like standard coordinates $(x, y)$, the top number of a vector is always horizontal (Left/Right) and the bottom number is always vertical (Up/Down).

quick_summary: Translation is a pure slide. Size, shape, and orientation never change.
Vector top number = Right (+) / Left (-).
Vector bottom number = Up (+) / Down (-).

ms_math_t12_st06.title: Rotation about a point
ms_math_t12_st06.overview: A rotation turns a shape around a fixed centre point. The shape keeps its size and shape; only its position and orientation change. To describe a rotation completely, specify the centre, angle and direction.

details: 1. **Centre of rotation:** The fixed point about which the shape turns (often the origin $(0,0)$).
2. **Angle:** The amount of the turn, such as $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ or $270^\circ$.
3. **Direction:** Clockwise or anticlockwise (counterclockwise).

key_concepts.definition: Coordinate shortcuts for rotations about the origin only.
details: **$90^\circ$ anticlockwise:** $(x,y)\rightarrow(-y,x)$.
**$90^\circ$ clockwise:** $(x,y)\rightarrow(y,-x)$.
**$180^\circ$ rotation:** $(x,y)\rightarrow(-x,-y)$.
These coordinate rules apply when the centre of rotation is the origin. A rotation about a different centre requires a different method.
Like reflection and translation, rotation is a rigid transformation. The rotated image is perfectly congruent to the original.

worked_examples.problem: Rotate the point $A(4, 1)$ by $90^\circ$ clockwise about the origin.
solution_steps: Step 1: A $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation about the origin uses $(x,y)\rightarrow(y,-x)$.
Step 2: Start with $A(4,1)$.
Step 3: Swap the coordinates to get $(1,4)$, then make the new $y$-coordinate negative.
Step 4: The image is $A'(1,-4)$.

worked_examples.problem: Rotate the point $C(-2, 5)$ by $180^\circ$ about the origin.
solution_steps: Step 1: A $180^\circ$ rotation about the origin uses $(x,y)\rightarrow(-x,-y)$.
Step 2: Start with $C(-2,5)$.
Step 3: Change the sign of each coordinate: $-2$ becomes $2$ and $5$ becomes $-5$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Mixing up the 90° clockwise and anticlockwise rules.
common_mistakes.correction: It is easy to forget which sign flips. If you are ever unsure, roughly plot the point on a graph and visually spin it a quarter turn. If you start in the top right (+, +) and spin clockwise, you must land in the bottom right (+, -). This visual check prevents sign errors.

quick_summary: Rotation turns a shape around a fixed point (usually the origin).
$180^\circ$ rotation flips both signs: $(x, y) \rightarrow (-x, -y)$.
A $270^\circ$ clockwise rotation is exactly the same as a $90^\circ$ anticlockwise rotation.

ms_math_t12_st07.title: Enlargement and reduction
ms_math_t12_st07.overview: Unlike translation, reflection, and rotation (which just move shapes around), enlargement and reduction actually change the size of the shape. These transformations stretch or shrink the shape proportionally, creating 'Similar' figures.

details: The scale factor $k$ tells you how each distance from the centre of enlargement changes.
If $k>1$, the image is an **enlargement**.
If $0<k<1$, the image is a **reduction**.
If $k=1$, the image is unchanged in size.
To find the length of a new side, multiply the original corresponding side by the scale factor: $\text{New Length} = \text{Original Length} \times k$.
A positive enlargement or reduction preserves all corresponding angles and keeps corresponding side lengths in the same ratio.
Every distance from the centre of enlargement is multiplied by the scale factor $k$.

visual_aids.title: Enlargement (Scale Factor = 2)
visual_aids.caption: Every side length doubles, but the overall shape and angles remain identical.
visual_aids.alt_text: Visual showing a small blue triangle with base 3 and height 4. Next to it is a larger green triangle with base 6 and height 8. Text says Scale Factor k = 2.

worked_examples.problem: A rectangle has a length of $6\text{ cm}$ and width of $4\text{ cm}$. It is enlarged using a scale factor of $2.5$. Find its new dimensions.
solution_steps: Step 1: Multiply the original length by the scale factor: $6 \times 2.5 = 15\text{ cm}$.
Step 2: Multiply the original width by the scale factor: $4 \times 2.5 = 10\text{ cm}$.

worked_examples.problem: A line segment originally measures $8\text{ cm}$. After enlargement, it measures $20\text{ cm}$. Find the scale factor.
solution_steps: Step 1: Use the formula: $k = \frac{\text{New}}{\text{Original}}$.
Step 2: Substitute the values: $k = \frac{20}{8}$.
Step 3: Simplify the fraction: $\frac{20}{8} = 2.5$.

common_mistakes.correction: A scale factor of $2$ means you MULTIPLY the sides by $2$. It does not mean you ADD $2\text{ cm}$ to every side.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dividing the original by the new to find $k$.
common_mistakes.correction: Always put the NEW size on top of the fraction. $k = \frac{\text{New}}{\text{Original}}$.

quick_summary: Enlargement ($k > 1$) makes things bigger.
Reduction ($k < 1$) makes things smaller.
Angles stay the same, but side lengths are multiplied by $k$.

ms_math_t12_st08.title: Scale factors in transformations
ms_math_t12_st08.overview: A scale factor changes lengths, perimeters, areas and volumes by different powers. For similar two-dimensional shapes, lengths and perimeters scale by $k$, while areas scale by $k^2$. For similar three-dimensional solids, surface areas scale by $k^2$ and volumes scale by $k^3$.

details: Every corresponding length is multiplied by the scale factor $k$. A perimeter, being a total boundary length, is therefore also multiplied by $k$.
Area is a two-dimensional measure. If both dimensions are multiplied by $k$, the area is multiplied by $k^2$.
The surface area of a similar three-dimensional solid also scales by $k^2$, because each face is a two-dimensional area.
For similar three-dimensional solids, all three dimensions are multiplied by $k$, so the volume is multiplied by $k^3$.

visual_aids.title: Scaling Across Dimensions
visual_aids.caption: How a scale factor of k=2 affects Length, Area, and Volume.
visual_aids.alt_text: Visual showing a table. Row 1: 1D Length -> scales by k. Row 2: 2D Area -> scales by k². Row 3: 3D Volume -> scales by k³.

worked_examples.problem: A square has an original area of $16\text{ cm}^2$. After enlargement, its area becomes $144\text{ cm}^2$. Find the length scale factor $k$.
solution_steps: Step 1: First, find the Area Scale Factor: $\frac{\text{New Area}}{\text{Original Area}} = \frac{144}{16} = 9$.
Step 2: The Area Scale Factor equals $k^2$. So, $k^2 = 9$.
Step 3: To find $k$, take the square root of $9$. $k = \sqrt{9} = 3$.

worked_examples.problem: A cube has an original volume of $8\text{ cm}^3$. It is enlarged by a length scale factor of $3$. What is its new volume?
solution_steps: Step 1: The length scale factor is $k=3$.
Step 2: For similar solids, the volume scale factor is $k^3=3^3=27$.
Step 3: Multiply the original volume by $27$: $8\times27=216$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Applying the length scale factor directly to the area or volume.
common_mistakes.correction: If sides double ($k=2$), area does NOT double. It gets multiplied by $2^2 = 4$. Volume gets multiplied by $2^3 = 8$.

quick_summary: Lengths and Perimeters change by $k$.
Areas change by $k^2$.
Volumes change by $k^3$.

ms_math_t12_st09.title: Describing transformations
ms_math_t12_st09.overview: In geometry exams, you will often be given a 'Before' and 'After' shape and asked to completely describe the transformation that took place. A full description requires specific mathematical vocabulary depending on the type of transformation.

details: State the word **Translation**.
Give the **translation vector** as a column vector. Its top entry is the horizontal shift and its bottom entry is the vertical shift.
State the word **Reflection**.
State the equation of the **Line of Reflection** (e.g., 'in the $y$-axis' or 'in the line $y=x$').
State the word **Rotation**.
Give all three requirements: The **Center of Rotation** (e.g., origin), the **Angle** (e.g., $90^\circ$), and the **Direction** (clockwise/anticlockwise).
State the word **Enlargement**.
State the **Center of Enlargement** and the **Scale Factor ($k$)**.

visual_aids.title: The Four Descriptions Checklist
visual_aids.caption: If you don't list all the required details, your description is incomplete.
visual_aids.alt_text: Visual showing a checklist. 1. Translation: Needs Vector. 2. Reflection: Needs Mirror Line. 3. Rotation: Needs Center, Angle, Direction. 4. Enlargement: Needs Center, Scale Factor.

worked_examples.problem: Under a translation, point $A(1,2)$ maps to $A'(5,7)$. Find the translation vector.
solution_steps: Step 1: Since the transformation is stated to be a translation, find the change in each coordinate.
Step 2: Horizontal change: $5-1=+4$.
Step 3: Vertical change: $7-2=+5$.
Step 4: Write the translation vector as a column vector.

worked_examples.problem: A point $P(3, 2)$ becomes $P'(-2, 3)$. Fully describe the transformation.
solution_steps: Step 1: The $x$ and $y$ swapped, and the first number became negative. This is the rule $(x, y) \rightarrow (-y, x)$.
Step 2: This rule belongs to a $90^\circ$ anticlockwise rotation about the origin.
worked_examples.final_answer: Rotation of $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about the origin $(0,0)$.

common_mistakes.correction: Writing 'It rotated $90^\circ$' will lose points. You must specify 'Rotation, $90^\circ$, anticlockwise, around the origin $(0,0)$'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing a Translation Vector with a Coordinate.
common_mistakes.correction: A vector is written stacked $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ and means 'move this much'. A coordinate $(4, 5)$ means 'this exact location'.

quick_summary: **Translation:** State Vector.
**Reflection:** State Mirror Line.
**Rotation:** State Center, Angle, Direction.
**Enlargement:** State Center, Scale Factor.

ms_math_t12_st10.title: Combining transformations
ms_math_t12_st10.overview: In geometry, you can string multiple transformations together like a chain reaction. The most important rule to remember is that the order in which you perform them matters immensely—swapping the order will often land your shape in a completely different final position.

details: Always apply the second transformation to the **intermediate image** (the shape generated by the first transformation), NEVER to the original starting shape.
Label your shapes to keep track: $A \rightarrow A' \rightarrow A''$.
Translating 3 units right then reflecting across the $y$-axis gives a very different result than reflecting across the $y$-axis first, then translating 3 units right.
**Translations:** Add the corresponding entries of the two translation vectors to find the combined vector.
**Enlargements:** When two enlargements have the same centre, multiply their scale factors to find the combined scale factor.

variables.k_1, k_2: Scale factors of two enlargements about the same centre

formulas.name: Adding Translation Vectors
formulas.equation: $$ \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} c \\ d \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a+c \\ b+d \end{pmatrix} $$

worked_examples.problem: A point $A(1, 2)$ is translated by vector $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$, and then translated again by vector $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$. Find its final position.
solution_steps: Step 1: Combine the two translation vectors by adding them.
Step 2: $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
Step 3: Apply the combined vector to the original point: $(1+5, 2+1) = (6, 3)$.

worked_examples.problem: A shape is enlarged by a scale factor of $4$ and then reduced by a scale factor of $0.5$ about the same center. What is the combined scale factor?
solution_steps: Step 1: Multiply the two scale factors together.
Step 2: $k_{\text{combined}} = 4 \times 0.5 = 2$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Applying the second transformation to the original shape.
common_mistakes.correction: Always apply Transformation #2 to the *image* produced by Transformation #1. It is a chain.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding scale factors instead of multiplying.
common_mistakes.correction: For two enlargements about the same centre, multiply the scale factors. If the first scale factor is $2$ and the second is $3$, the combined scale factor is $2\times3=6$, not $2+3=5$.

quick_summary: Transformations are sequential. Always use the new intermediate coordinates for the next step.
Order matters. Translation then Reflection $\neq$ Reflection then Translation.
Add translation vectors. Multiply scale factors.

ms_math_t12_st11.title: Congruence through transformations
ms_math_t12_st11.overview: Transformations are the physical proof behind congruence. If you can slide, spin, or flip one shape so that it perfectly covers another shape, you have proven beyond a doubt that the two shapes are completely congruent.

details: **Translations, Reflections, and Rotations** are called rigid transformations. They move the shape but freeze its size and angles.
If a shape undergoes any combination of these three transformations, the final image is ALWAYS congruent to the original.
An enlargement with a positive scale factor $k\ne1$ changes the size. It preserves similarity, but the image is not congruent to the original.
A scale factor of $1$ leaves the size unchanged.

key_concepts.definition: Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Congruent.
details: Once you prove two triangles are congruent (e.g., by matching them up after a reflection), you automatically know that all their matching sides and matching angles are exactly equal.

visual_aids.title: Rigid Transformations Preserve Congruence
visual_aids.caption: No matter how you flip or spin it, the core dimensions of the triangle never change.
visual_aids.alt_text: Visual showing three identical triangles. One is translated, one is rotated, one is reflected. All say 'Congruent (Same Size & Shape)'.

worked_examples.problem: A triangle with sides $3\text{ cm}, 4\text{ cm}, 5\text{ cm}$ is reflected across the $x$-axis, then translated $5$ units right. Are the original and final triangles congruent?
solution_steps: Step 1: Check the transformations used. Reflection and Translation are both rigid transformations (isometries).
Step 2: Rigid transformations preserve size and shape.
Step 3: Therefore, the final triangle is perfectly congruent to the original.

worked_examples.problem: A square is enlarged by a scale factor of $2$ and then translated $3$ units down. Is the final square congruent to the original?
solution_steps: Step 1: The translation preserves size, but the enlargement changes the size.
Step 2: Because the scale factor is $2$ (not $1$), the new square is twice as large.
Step 3: They share the same shape, making them Similar, but they are different sizes, so they are not Congruent.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking a flipped shape is no longer congruent.
common_mistakes.correction: Congruence doesn't care about orientation. A left hand is a perfect mirror image of a right hand. In geometry, they are considered congruent.

quick_summary: Rigid Transformations = Translation, Rotation, Reflection.
Rigid Transformations ALWAYS result in Congruent shapes.
Enlargement (where $k \neq 1$) destroys congruence but maintains similarity.

ms_math_t12_st12.title: Tessellations and repeating patterns
ms_math_t12_st12.overview: A tessellation covers a flat surface completely with one or more repeating shapes, leaving no gaps and no overlaps. Tessellations are used in patterns such as floor tiles, brickwork and honeycombs.

details: At each point where tiles meet, the angles around that point must add up to exactly $360^\circ$ for the tiles to fit without gaps or overlaps.
A tessellation may use one tile shape or a repeating combination of different shapes.

There are exactly three regular polygons that each tessellate the plane by themselves: **equilateral triangles** ($6\times60^\circ=360^\circ$), **squares** ($4\times90^\circ=360^\circ$), and **regular hexagons** ($3\times120^\circ=360^\circ$).

key_concepts.concept: Why a regular pentagon does not tessellate by itself
key_concepts.definition: Its interior angle does not divide evenly into 360°.
details: Each interior angle of a regular pentagon is $108^\circ$. Three angles make $324^\circ$, leaving a $36^\circ$ gap; four make $432^\circ$, which is too much.
Therefore, regular pentagons cannot form a regular tessellation by themselves.

formulas.name: Tessellation Vertex Rule
formulas.equation: $$ \text{Sum of interior angles at meeting point} = 360^\circ $$

worked_examples.problem: Can you create a regular tessellation using only regular octagons?
solution_steps: Step 1: The interior angle of a regular octagon is $135^\circ$.
Step 2: Try to fit them around a vertex to equal $360^\circ$.
Step 3: Two octagons $= 135 \times 2 = 270^\circ$.
Step 4: Three octagons $= 135 \times 3 = 405^\circ$.
Step 5: $270$ leaves a gap. $405$ overlaps. There is no way to perfectly hit $360^\circ$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming any repeating pattern is a tessellation.
common_mistakes.correction: A repeating pattern is not necessarily a tessellation. For example, a row of circles repeats, but gaps remain between them. A tessellation must cover the surface completely with no gaps or overlaps.

quick_summary: A tessellation covers a flat surface with no gaps and no overlaps.
The angles meeting at each vertex add to $360^\circ$.
The only regular polygons that tessellate the plane by themselves are equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons.
